strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: first to reconstruct full hyperspectral images from grayscale measurements using only a phase-only lens, addressing a challenging and practically relevant imaging scenario

Technically sound approach: clever solution to patch-based ambiguity through PSF-guided sampling; demonstrates that patch sizes as small as PSF support suffice with proper global consistency constraints

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive comparisons against 8 baselines, thorough ablations (Table 2), systematic PSF design analysis with saliency visualizations, cross-dataset generalization tests, and noise robustness analysis
Strong empirical results: 34.63 dB PSNR surpasses next-best baseline by 2.86 dB with superior SSIM (0.94 vs 0.90) and SAM (0.11 vs 0.15) metrics across multiple evaluation frameworks
Valuable uncertainty quantification: provides per-pixel uncertainty estimates that meaningfully correlate with reconstruction error (r=0.80), adding practical utility beyond point estimates

Excellent reproducibility: detailed supplementary material includes complete optical design theory, pseudocode, model configuration (Table 5), training details, and interpretability analysis via saliency maps showing learned PSF structure
weaknesses: Purely simulation-based validation: all experiments use rendered measurements from forward optical model with no real optical demonstrations; metalens designs claimed 'physically realizable' but experimentally unvalidated; real measurements may exhibit systematic deviations from model assumptions (unmodeled aberrations, alignment errors, wavelength-dependent effects) that could significantly impact practical feasibility

Patch scale ambiguity requires workaround: individual patch max-normalization creates ambiguity necessitating per-patch least-squares scale recovery (Eq. 4); suggests problem formulation could be refined; post-hoc scale correction indicates model learns incomplete information

Significant computational cost: ~22.7 seconds per 256×256 image due to 20 guidance iterations; O(n² log n) complexity limits practical deployment; guidance remains main bottleneck with no adaptive allocation strategy addressed

Degraded cross-dataset generalization: performance drops from 34.63 dB (ARAD1K) to 33.48 dB (ICVL, 1280×1280) to 32.37 dB (Harvard, 1024×1344) despite claims of 'generalization without finetuning'; suggests overfitting to training distribution despite limited data (900 images)

Heavy dependence on guidance for ill-posed problem: 2.31 dB improvement from guidance (32.32→34.63 dB) indicates problem remains highly ill-posed even with diffusion model; unclear robustness to PSF mismatch or optical parameter uncertainty

Limited methodological novelty: patch-based diffusion and measurement guidance are established techniques; primary contribution is application to this specific problem rather than novel ML methodology; should arguably be classified as Applied/Systems contribution

Incomplete practical analysis: metalens efficiency ~80% varying with wavelength (impact on SNR unanalyzed), wavelength range limited to 400-700nm, shift-invariant PSF assumption not validated across field, manufacturing tolerances ignored, sensor calibration requirements unspecified

Baseline comparison limitations: eight baseline methods not originally designed for this minimalist scenario and trained from scratch with minimal modifications; no diffusion-based baselines; architectural advantages favor proposed patch-based approach when compared at fixed resolution
Uncertainty estimates lack principled Bayesian foundation: variance-based estimates don't distinguish aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty; calibration not analyzed; correlation r=0.80 is moderate

Missing technical justifications: loss function choice (L1-epsilon) lacks ablation; why spatial attention outperforms spectral attention for 31-channel data only briefly mentioned; saliency resemblance to PSF is expected but doesn't deeply validate learned physics

strengths: Novel problem formulation combining optical design with learning: demonstrates feasible HSI reconstruction from single grayscale measurement using diffractive metasurface, addressing a genuinely challenging and under-explored scenario
Strong experimental validation with real prototype: includes fabricated metasurface, measured PSF validation, and achieves 34.63 dB PSNR outperforming comparable methods on ARADIK dataset

Comprehensive experimental analysis: thorough ablations on PSF designs/patch sizes/guidance iterations, saliency analysis revealing learned optical structures, per-wavelength uncertainty correlating with error (r=0.69-0.80)
Physically-grounded approach: optical model well-founded in Fourier optics; guided sampling cleverly enforces measurement consistency during inference using camera PSF as constraint
Good cross-dataset generalization and scalability: demonstrates generalization to ICVL/Harvard/CAVE datasets; patch-based approach scales to arbitrary image sizes without retraining

Clear presentation with extensive documentation: well-written paper with effective visualizations and detailed supplementary material covering metasurface design, implementation details, and additional results
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation with homogeneous regions: method fails significantly on spectrally uniform patches lacking spatial variation; this reflects inherent weakness of local patch processing without global spectral context, limiting applicability to diverse scenes

Impractical computational cost: 22 seconds per 256×256 image, up to 52 minutes for 1024×1344 scenes, with ~20 guidance iterations per diffusion step; makes real-time or near real-time imaging infeasible

Limited practical feasibility: requires specialized metasurface fabrication; tabletop experimental setup with controlled illumination far from deployment scenarios; specialized hardware requirements limit broader adoption

Incomplete justification of design choices: choice among 8 PSF designs appears empirical; limited principled methodology for metasurface optimization; unclear how to extend approach to different optical systems without major redesign

Reproducibility and data accessibility concerns: no mention of code or data release; requires paired HSI ground truth for training; limited analysis of sensitivity to domain gap from training distribution

Insufficient analysis of guidance mechanism: interaction between patch-level learning and full-field optical consistency underdeveloped; gradient descent step count (30-60) lacks principled justification; potential for optimization instability not discussed

Limited comparative context: comparisons primarily with general HSI reconstruction methods not designed for this measurement model; no controlled comparison with other snapshot HSI approaches (CASSI, filter arrays); assessment of when guidance is essential vs. optional missing

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Reconstructing HSI from filterless single-shot measurements using only a diffractive lens and panchromatic sensor is genuinely underexplored and challenging.
Physics-informed approach: Well-motivated integration of optical PSF-based guidance with learning-based diffusion models to enforce physical consistency across patch reconstructions.
Experimental prototype validation: Includes actual fabricated metalens prototype with experimental measurements, adding credibility beyond simulation-only studies.
Comprehensive evaluation: Includes ablation studies on patch size, guidance iterations, PSF designs, cross-dataset generalization tests, and uncertainty quantification.
Technical depth and reproducibility: Rigorous mathematical formulation, detailed architectural specifications, training protocols, and pseudo-code enhance reproducibility.
Useful uncertainty estimates: Per-pixel uncertainty predictions correlate well with reconstruction error, potentially useful for practitioners.
weaknesses: Significant simulation-to-reality gap: Real prototype PSNR (~31.2 dB) substantially lower than simulation (~34.6 dB); visible artifacts (ringing, color shifts) appear in experimental results; requires LoRA finetuning to achieve acceptable real-world performance, indicating poor generalization.

Severely limited real-world validation: Only 8 tabletop scenes with controlled indoor setups; no comparison to commercial HSI systems; reference imagery captured with separate optical system requiring imperfect geometric/spectral alignment.
Prohibitive computational cost: ~48-hour training on H100 GPU; inference requires 13-52 minutes per scene, making practical deployment infeasible for most applications.

Fundamental method limitations: Patch-based formulation fails on large homogeneous regions (acknowledged and demonstrated); requires knowledge of exact system PSF (limits portability); inherent texture dependency; resolution tied to training data requiring retraining.

Weak baseline comparisons: Compared methods (SSiM, MST-L, DAUHST) designed for RGB-to-HSI or compressed sensing tasks, not ideal for filterless measurement reconstruction; no comparison to other filterless HSI approaches.

Poor cross-dataset generalization: Significant uncertainty increases in cross-dataset evaluation (Fig. 5); per-wavelength performance varies substantially; cannot handle scenes outside training distribution without adaptation.

Incomplete practical analysis: Limited discussion of failure modes beyond homogeneous regions; uncertainty calibration on real data not thoroughly validated; texture requirement rarely justified; missing failure mode analysis.

Presentation and disclosure: Critical real-world performance degradation not emphasized upfront; practical limitations relegated to brief Sec. 6; real-to-sim performance gap suggests simulation may inadequately capture real-world challenges.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: recovering full 31-channel HSI from single filterless grayscale snapshot via flat optics is underexplored and practically valuable
Innovative physics-guided diffusion approach: elegant integration of optical PSF constraints with patch-based conditional diffusion models to enforce consistency, bridging optics and deep learning

Comprehensive experimental validation: simulation on multiple datasets (ARADIK 34.63 dB PSNR, +2.86 dB vs. prior art), cross-dataset generalization (ICVL, Harvard), and physical prototype with fabricated metasurface

Rigorous experimental methodology: detailed metasurface fabrication, PSF measurement/calibration procedures, controlled ablations (guidance iterations, patch sizes, PSF designs), and interpretability analysis via saliency maps
Uncertainty quantification: per-pixel uncertainty maps computed from sample variation, with moderate-to-strong correlation with reconstruction error (r=0.80 simulation, r=0.69 experimental)
Technical soundness: correct mathematical formulations, proper noise modeling (Gaussian + shot), well-justified patch normalization, and ablations supporting design choices
Extensive ablation studies demonstrating that patch-level guidance is more effective than simply scaling the diffusion model, with clear evidence for design decisions
Reproducibility strengths: algorithm pseudocode, detailed hyperparameters, multiple datasets, supplementary material comprehensively documenting experimental setup and calibration
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (method pipeline, experimental results, cross-dataset generalizations) and well-organized supplementary material
weaknesses: Limited scale of physical experiments: only 8 tabletop scenes captured with fabricated prototype from restricted central region (~10% of sensor FOV); no quantitative evaluation against commercial HSI cameras on experimental data

Known fundamental limitation on spatial homogeneity: explicitly documented failure on large uniform regions where patches lack spatial-spectral variation (Fig. 9); standard mitigation (smaller patches) worsens ill-posedness

Optical model assumptions not fully validated: PSF shift-invariance only verified in central region; field-dependent aberrations, sensor nonlinearity, and dynamic range limitations not modeled; scalability to full FOV unclear

Restricted spectral and domain scope: fixed to 31 visible channels (400-700 nm); not evaluated on NIR/SWIR or non-natural-scene domains (medical, industrial, microscopy); cross-domain generalization (CASSI) requires LoRA finetuning

Computational cost and practical deployment concerns: 22 sec/scene (ARADIK), 52 min (higher-res datasets); no wall-clock time comparisons vs. baselines; guidance loop complexity not fully analyzed; real-time use unclear

Incomplete baseline comparisons: prior methods (CASSI, coded aperture) designed for different optical systems; most baselines from 2020-2021; no comparison with recent diffusion-based HSI methods; simple baseline justification sparse

Moderate experimental uncertainty calibration: Pearson correlation with error drops from 0.80 (simulation) to 0.69 (experimental data); limited guidance on when uncertainty estimates are trustworthy; uncertainty from sample variation, not fully Bayesian

Circular calibration dependency: PSF measurement requires tunable laser and careful alignment; experimental calibration procedure (Sec. 2.4) requires ground-truth HSI reference images, creating practical deployment bottleneck

Limited statistical rigor: small experimental sample (N=8 scenes); no confidence intervals or significance tests on cross-dataset metrics; dataset bias toward natural scenes with spectral variation; noise model simplifications

Important methodological details relegated to supplementary material: patch normalization strategy critical to resolving scale ambiguity but not sufficiently prominent in main text; connection between patch-level training and field-level inference needs clearer intuition
